stimulus.text: Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank, February 1791: “To take a single step beyond the boundaries thus specially drawn around the powers of Congress, is to take possession of a boundless field of power, no longer susceptible of any definition.” Paraphrase: Hamilton answered that the Constitution’s necessary and proper clause allowed Congress to charter a bank. President Washington signed the bank bill into law in February 1791.
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank, February 1791; Alexander Hamilton, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank, February 1791. Public domain.

stem: What did President Washington decide in the debate over the national bank?

options.text: He vetoed the bank bill and asked Congress to amend the Constitution.
options.misconception: Washington did not veto the bill; the stimulus says he signed it.

options.text: He signed the bank bill into law, siding with Hamilton’s broad reading.
He sent the question to the Supreme Court for a ruling.
options.misconception: Washington decided the question himself; it did not go to the Court.

options.text: He refused to act and let the bill die without his signature.
options.misconception: The stimulus says Washington signed the bill into law in February 1791.

rationales.B: The stimulus says Washington signed the bank bill into law in February 1791, accepting Hamilton’s reading.
rationales.A: Washington did not veto the bill; the stimulus says he signed it.
rationales.C: Background: the Supreme Court did not rule on the bank in 1791; Washington decided himself.
rationales.D: The stimulus says Washington signed the bill, so he did not let it die.
rationales.general:
1. Jefferson argued the bank went beyond Congress’s listed powers, while Hamilton defended it under the necessary and proper clause.
2. The stimulus says Washington signed the bank bill into law in February 1791.
3. Signing the bill meant accepting Hamilton’s broad reading over Jefferson’s strict one.
4. So Washington settled the debate in Hamilton’s favor, at least for that moment.
Remember: when a president signs a disputed bill, the signature is the decision.
